hints: Think about what mass you are adding up when the substance is ionic, so you use formula units rather than single molecules.
Remember all relative masses have no units because they are compared to a standard, think what that standard atom and value is.
walkthrough:
Sort out formula versus molecular**
For an ionic lattice like $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{Fe}(\text{SO}_4)_2$ there are no discrete molecules, so you talk about one formula unit. Add up the masses of all the atoms or ions shown in that formula. Because isotopes exist you use the weighted average mass.

Add the relative scale**
Relative means ratio with no units. The worldwide standard is the $^{12}\text{C}$ atom. Take exactly one twelfth of its mass as 1 unit, so carbon-12 itself is defined as exactly 12. Your $M_r$ of 284 means one formula unit is 284 times heavier than that standard unit.

Final answer: The (weighted) average mass of a formula unit / molecule
compared to 1/12 the mass of an atom of carbon-12.

hints: Count outer electrons first, N has 5 and each H has 1, and remember the + charge means one electron has been lost overall.
Think which atom supplies both electrons in the fourth N-H bond that forms when $\text{NH}_3$ bonds to $\text{H}^+$.
walkthrough:
Set up the electron count**
Nitrogen is in Group 15 so it brings 5 outer electrons, shown as $\times$. Each hydrogen brings 1 electron, shown as $\bullet$. In $\text{NH}_3$, three N-H pairs are already shared. When $\text{H}^+$ attaches, it brings no electron, so nitrogen donates its lone pair.

Draw the four identical bonds correctly**
Place N in the centre with four H around it. Draw four shared pairs between N and each H. For three of them show $\times + \bullet$. For the dative bond show $\times + \times$ to prove both electrons came from nitrogen. Put square brackets around the whole ion with a + charge outside, and show outer shell electrons only.

Final answer: Central N surrounded by 4 H atoms, each N-H bond shown as a shared pair. Three shared pairs shown as one dot + one cross, one shared pair shown as two crosses (both electrons from N). Overall + charge shown.

hints: Count bonding pairs and lone pairs on N in $\text{NH}_4^+$, compare with $\text{NH}_3$ which has a lone pair.
Recall the ideal angle when four electron pairs spread out equally in three dimensions to minimise repulsion.
walkthrough:
Apply electron pair repulsion**
In $\text{NH}_4^+$ nitrogen has four bonding pairs and zero lone pairs. All four pairs repel equally, so they point to the corners of a tetrahedron. This is the same electron geometry as methane, $\text{CH}_4$.

Give the ideal angle**
With four equal repulsions and no lone pair to squeeze the angle, the H-N-H angle is the perfect tetrahedral angle of $109.5^{\circ}$. Do not confuse this with $\text{NH}_3$, which is pyramidal with $107^{\circ}$ because its lone pair repels more strongly.

Final answer: shape: tetrahedral
bond angle: $109.5^{\circ}$ (accept $109$ to $109.5^{\circ}$)

hints: Split the phrase in two, think what weak means in terms of how many acid particles release $\text{H}^+$ in water.
Recall the Bronsted-Lowry definition is about transfer of a specific particle, think proton versus electron versus hydroxide.
walkthrough:
Explain weak**
Strong acids dissociate almost completely. A weak acid sets up an equilibrium lying far to the left, so only a small fraction of $\text{NH}_4^+$ molecules release $\text{H}^+$ at any time. Most stays as $\text{NH}_4^+$.

Explain Bronsted-Lowry acid**
Bronsted and Lowry defined acids and bases by proton transfer. An acid is simply a proton donor, meaning it gives $\text{H}^+$ to another species such as water. Here $\text{NH}_4^+$ donates a proton to become $\text{NH}_3$.

Final answer: weak: partially / incompletely dissociates or ionises in solution
Bronsted-Lowry acid: proton ($\text{H}^+$) donor

hints: Identify the proton acceptor, water accepts $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{NH}_4^+$ to form $\text{NH}_3$ and what oxonium species.
Remember weak acids give equilibrium arrows and every aqueous species needs a correct state symbol.
walkthrough:
Build the proton transfer**
$\text{NH}_4^+$ donates $\text{H}^+$ to $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. That gives the conjugate base $\text{NH}_3$ plus $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$. Check atoms and charge: both sides have N1, H6, O1 and +1 charge, so it balances.

Add equilibrium and states**
Because it is a weak acid the reaction is reversible, so use $\rightleftharpoons$ not a single arrow. $\text{NH}_4^+$ is dissolved, so (aq), water as solvent is (l), $\text{NH}_3$ dissolved is (aq), and $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ dissolved is (aq).
Final answer: $\text{NH}_4^+(\text{aq}) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l}) \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_3(\text{aq}) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(\text{aq})$

hints: Track electrons, Mn falls from +7 to +2 (gain of 5e-) while each Fe rises from +2 to +3 (loss of 1e-), so think what ratio balances electron transfer.
walkthrough:
Balance using electron change**
Mn in $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is +7 and becomes $\text{Mn}^{2+}$, a drop of 5, so 5 electrons gained. Each $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ loses 1 electron, so you need 5 $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ for every 1 $\text{MnO}_4^-$. Then balance O with 4 $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and H with 8 $\text{H}^+$. Charge also balances at +17 each side.
Final answer: $\text{MnO}_4^-(\text{aq}) + 5\text{Fe}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 8\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + 5\text{Fe}^{3+}(\text{aq}) + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})$

hints: Decide if $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is oxidised or reduced by looking at whether it becomes $\text{Fe}^{3+}$.
Link that change to electrons and oxidation number to justify the term reducing agent.
walkthrough:
Spot oxidation**
$\text{Fe}^{2+}$ changes to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$. Losing a negatively charged electron makes the ion more positive, so this is oxidation.

Name the role**
A species that is itself oxidised causes the other species to be reduced by giving it electrons. That is exactly what a reducing agent does. So $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ reduces $\text{MnO}_4^-$ to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ while it is oxidised.

Final answer: $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is a reducing agent / reductant
because it donates / loses electrons (to $\text{MnO}_4^-$) / its oxidation number increases / it is oxidised to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$

hints: Convert $20.0 \text{ cm}^3$ to $\text{dm}^3$ and apply $n = cV$ for the manganate(VII) solution.
walkthrough:
Apply $n = cV$**
$$V = 20.0 \text{ cm}^3 = 0.0200 \text{ dm}^3$$
$$n = cV = 0.0200 \text{ mol dm}^{-3} \times 0.0200 \text{ dm}^3 = 4.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$
This is the amount of $\text{MnO}_4^-$ that reacted.
Final answer: $$n(\text{MnO}_4^-) = 0.0200 \times \frac{20.0}{1000} = 4.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$

hints: Use the balanced equation ratio, 1 $\text{MnO}_4^-$ reacts with 5 $\text{Fe}^{2+}$, to scale up your answer from (iii).
walkthrough:
Scale by the mole ratio**
From the equation:
$$\frac{n(\text{Fe}^{2+})}{n(\text{MnO}_4^-)} = \frac{5}{1}$$
$$n(\text{Fe}^{2+}) = 5 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-4} = 2.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$
This is also the amount of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ in the $0.784 \text{ g}$ sample, since all of the solution was titrated.

hints: One mole of hydrated salt contains one mole of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$, so use $M_r = m/n$ with $m = 0.784 \text{ g}$ and your $n$ from (iv).
walkthrough:
Link salt moles to iron moles**
Formula $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{Fe}(\text{SO}_4)_2 \cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}$ contains 1 Fe per formula unit, so:
$$n(\text{salt}) = n(\text{Fe}^{2+}) = 2.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$
$$M_r = \frac{m}{n} = \frac{0.784 \text{ g}}{2.0 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}} = 392$$
Final answer: $$M_r = \frac{0.784}{2.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 392$$

hints: Subtract the anhydrous $M_r$ of 284 from 392 to leave the mass due to water, then divide by $M_r(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = 18$.
walkthrough:
Isolate the water mass**
Total hydrated $M_r = 392$. Anhydrous $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{Fe}(\text{SO}_4)_2 = 284$.
Mass due to water:
$$392 - 284 = 108$$
Each water is 18:
$$x = \frac{108}{18} = 6$$
So the formula is $(\text{NH}_4)_2\text{Fe}(\text{SO}_4)_2 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
